newsitem.title: YEMEN: Campaigning begins for Yemen elections.
newsitem.headline: Campaigning begins for Yemen elections.

text.p: Candidates on Monday began campaigning for Yemen's April 27 parliamentary poll, the first since a 1994 civil war nearly tore apart the Arab state.

The candidates, seeking votes for 301 parliamentary seats under the banners of 12 parties or as independents, began hanging posters and pictures on the walls of buildings and appealing to Yemenis on television and radio.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose former leaders launched the southern separatist campaign that sparked the war, and four others have announced they will boycott the poll because of alleged irregularities.
But Abdel Bari Taher, a member of the YSP leadership, told Reuters that about 20 party members would run as independents.
Another YSP official said between 50 and 60 members from the middle and lower-level leadership have also announced their candidacy as independents.
The move has raised concerns among some YSP officials.

"I urge the candidates from the party who have nominated themselves as independents to withdraw because the party's position to boycott the election should be adhered to by everyone," said YSP secretary general Ali Saleh Obad in a statement published in al-Thawri, the party newspaper.
Some 4.6 million of the 7.5 million people aged 18 and over who are eligible to vote out of a population of 16 million had registered for the poll when the process ended last August.
The YSP won 50 seats in the outgoing assembly, dominated by the General People's Congress (GPC) of President Ali Abdullah Saleh and its junior coalition partner the Islamist Islah Party.
Western diplomats expect the GPC to return as the governing party and then move further to meet World Bank demands for economic reforms, a sensitive subject in Yemen.
The higher election committee has announced that 3,804 candidates, including 20 women, are running in the poll. Forty-four women ran in the 1993 election.
Saleh has invited international observers to Yemen to ensure a fair ballot and the first four arrived from Britain earlier this month.
International observers monitored the last poll in 1993 when 22 parties competed for 301 seats in parliament.

Faris al-Sanabani, chairman of the Sanaa-based Arab Democratic Institute, said he expected about 70 international observers from the United States and Europe to arrive in the coming days ahead of the poll.
A fractious republic with a vigorous but fragmented opposition, Yemen is a small independent oil producer on the southern border of Saudi Arabia.
